You're converting 6 games on Nxeon (VPS/game-hosting platform, Next.js/Prisma/Postgres, staging tree at /opt/nxeon-staging — work ONLY in staging, never /opt/nxeon prod. Never run `npm run build`; verify with `npx tsc --noEmit` only) from self-managed-VPS products into genuine managed one-click hosting, matching the pattern already proven today for 12+ new games.

Context: a prior investigation found these 6 existing games are currently sold as generic VPS with root SSH access — the customer has to manually SteamCMD-install the dedicated server themselves, with generic "Standard/Pro/Max" pricing tiers instead of real game-specific provisioning: **ARK: Survival Evolved (family `ark`), Satisfactory, Project Zomboid, 7 Days to Die, V Rising, Conan Exiles**. Their `prisma/seed-wave1-games.ts`/`seed-wave2-games.ts` files apparently already contain `GamePlan`/`OsTemplate` seed code describing what a managed one-click version WOULD look like — but it was confirmed those rows were never actually seeded into the DB (0 rows for these families on staging). Read those two seed files FIRST to see exactly what was already written/planned.

The owner's directive: they want game server deploys to be as close to "click pay → server is ready to play" as possible, with zero manual customer steps. These 6 games currently fail that completely (customer manually installs everything). Fix this by making them real managed one-click products, following the EXACT pattern already proven today in `prisma/seed-wave3-games.ts` and `seed-wave4-games.ts` (community Docker image wrapping SteamCMD, `OsTemplate.setupScript` via cloud-init, reusing the existing generic `worker/game-control.ts` start/stop/backup machinery).

Your job, per game:
1. Read the wave1/wave2 seed file's existing plan for this game (App ID, intended tiers) as your starting point — verify the App ID and pricing are still sensible/current (SteamCMD app IDs don't change, but check for updates), don't blindly trust old seed-file drafts without a sanity check.
2. Find a trustworthy, actively-maintained community Docker image for automated SteamCMD install+launch (check Docker Hub/GHCR, prefer publishers already trusted in this codebase where a precedent exists — e.g. check if any of these 6 games already have a known-good image referenced anywhere, even in comments).
3. Create/finish the `OsTemplate` row with a real, working cloud-init `setupScript` (this is the meat of the work — the script needs to actually pull the image, mount a data volume, configure the game's dedicated-server config file with sensible defaults, and start it automatically on boot with zero customer interaction beyond picking a tier and paying).
4. Seed real `GamePlan` pricing tiers (reuse the wave1/2 draft numbers if they still look reasonable relative to comparable games already live, adjust if not).
5. Wire `lib/games.ts`/`lib/game-control.ts` (these families likely already have entries since they're pre-existing games — just need the provisioning-side wiring, not new family registration) and add to a new `prisma/seed-wave7-games.ts` (or extend an existing wave file if more consistent with the codebase's convention — use your judgment) with the OsTemplate+GamePlan rows.
6. Seed against staging DB, verify each family now has active `GamePlan` rows with valid `osTemplateId` and passes the same `withTiers` deploy-wizard check used for every other game today.
7. Run `npx tsc --noEmit`, keep clean throughout — this is 6 games, pace yourself for correctness.

Do NOT touch /opt/nxeon (prod). Do NOT remove or break the existing self-managed-VPS option if customers might already be using it for these games in prod — this is purely ADDING the real managed one-click path on staging; do not delete the old VPS-based purchase path's underlying data/code. If any of the 6 games turns out to have a real blocker (e.g., the community Docker ecosystem for it is genuinely unreliable/unmaintained, or licensing issues), stop for that game and report it clearly rather than shipping something broken.

Report back (table, under 500 words): per-game status (fully converted to one-click/orderable now, or blocked-and-why), App ID, Docker image used, pricing tiers seeded (vs. the old wave1/2 draft numbers, note if you changed them and why), and final `tsc` status.

async function main() {
  const templateIdByFamily = new Map<string, string>();
  let sort = 90;
  for (const t of TEMPLATES) {
    const os = await db.osTemplate.upsert({
      where: { slug: t.family },
      create: {
        slug: t.family, name: t.name, category: "APPLICATION", family: t.family, version: "", logo: t.family,
        vmid: 9000, baseVmid: 9000, setupScript: t.setupScript, minRamMB: t.minRamMB, minDiskGB: t.minDiskGB,

      },
      update: { name: t.name, setupScript: t.setupScript, minRamMB: t.minRamMB, minDiskGB: t.minDiskGB, active: true },
    });
    templateIdByFamily.set(t.family, os.id);
    console.log(`  osTemplate ${t.family.padEnd(16)} → ${os.id}`);
  }

  const plans = await db.plan.findMany({ where: { active: true }, orderBy: { ramMB: "asc" } });
  if (plans.length === 0) throw new Error("No active VPS plans — run the main seed first.");
  const largest = plans[plans.length - 1];

  let created = 0, updated = 0;
  const sortByGame = new Map<string, number>();
  for (const spec of TIERS) {
    const basePlan = plans.find((p) => p.ramMB >= spec.ramMB) ?? largest;
    const osId = templateIdByFamily.get(spec.gameFamily) ?? null;
    const sortOrder = sortByGame.get(spec.gameFamily) ?? 0;
    sortByGame.set(spec.gameFamily, sortOrder + 1);
    const data = {
      gameFamily: spec.gameFamily, name: spec.name, ramMB: spec.ramMB, cpuCores: spec.cpuCores, diskGB: spec.diskGB,
      slots: spec.slots, priceCents: spec.priceCents, termMonths: 1, basePlanId: basePlan.id, osTemplateId: osId,
      featured: spec.featured ?? false, active: true, sortOrder,
    };
    const existing = await db.gamePlan.findFirst({ where: { gameFamily: spec.gameFamily, name: spec.name } });
    if (existing) { await db.gamePlan.update({ where: { id: existing.id }, data }); updated++; }
    else { await db.gamePlan.create({ data }); created++; }
    console.log(`  plan ${spec.name.padEnd(38)} base=${basePlan.name}`);
  }
  console.log(`\nWave 7: ${TEMPLATES.length} OsTemplates, GamePlans ${created} created / ${updated} updated.`);
}

main().catch((e) => { console.error(e); process.exit(1); }).finally(() => db.$disconnect());

## Default Ports

Enshrouded uses UDP port 15636 for game traffic and 15637 for queries by default.

## Firewall Configuration

You need to add incoming rules to your Windows Firewall to allow TCP/UDP port 15636 (game port) and 15637 (Steam query port). Both must be forwarded and allowed through your firewall for friends to connect.

## Windows Firewall Rules

For Windows, you can use PowerShell commands to create the necessary firewall rules: New-NetFirewallRule commands for both TCP and UDP protocols on ports 15636 and 15637 for inbound and outbound traffic.

## Router Port Forwarding

Forward the game port (15636 by default) and query port on your router to the server machine, and allow them through the OS firewall. You can access your router's control panel by typing "192.168.0.1" in your browser's search bar.

## Configuration File

All configuration is done inside the enshrouded_server.json file at the base folder. If you use non-standard ports, you'll need to open the ports that you designated in the configuration file.
